title: How to Lead Volunteers Without Using Them Up
subtitle: A pastoral guide to recruiting, equipping, and releasing church volunteers so they serve from calling instead of guilt and last for years instead of months.

sections.title: The Church Runs on People We Forget to Thank
sections.body:
Every church has a quiet machine underneath it. The people who set up chairs at six in the morning. The woman who has run the nursery for nineteen years. The man who counts the offering when everyone else has gone home. The whole thing depends on them, and most of them are tired.

The temptation for every leader is to see volunteers as labor instead of people. There is a need, they fill it, and we are grateful in the way you are grateful for a tool that works. We stop asking how they are doing and start asking whether they can take one more thing. And they can, usually, because they love the church and they do not want to say no, and so we keep adding until the day they quietly disappear and we wonder what happened.

Not staff you do not pay. Saints you are called to shepherd. The moment a volunteer becomes a resource to be spent rather than a soul to be tended, you have stopped being their pastor and started being their employer, and you are not even paying them. That is the line. Cross it often enough and you will burn through the most faithful people in your church while telling yourself they were happy to help.

sections.title: Recruit to a Calling, Not a Vacancy
sections.body:
Most volunteer recruiting is desperation dressed as opportunity. The slot is empty, the leader is anxious, and so the announcement goes out, and whoever feels guilty enough raises a hand. That is how you fill a role. It is not how you call a worker.

There is a better way, and it is slower. Instead of begging the room, you watch the room. You notice who is already drawn to children, who carries grief well, who cannot sit still while a need goes unmet. Then you go to that person and you do not ask them to fill a hole. You tell them what you have seen God put in them, and you invite them to use it. People will say no to a vacancy and yes to a calling, because one treats them as a body and the other treats them as a gift.

Jesus did not post a sign-up sheet. He went and found Peter at his nets and named what Peter would become. Specific, personal, unhurried calling builds workers who stay. The mass appeal builds a roster that turns over every year. Recruit the way the Lord recruited you. He did not need a warm body. He wanted you.

sections.title: Do Not Drop People Into the Deep End
sections.body:
We recruit a volunteer, hand them a key and a curriculum, and walk away relieved that the slot is filled. Then we are surprised when they quit in March. We never equipped them. We deployed them.

Equipping is the work between yes and competence, and it is the work most churches skip. It means someone shadows the new greeter for a month before they greet alone. It means the new small group leader watches a seasoned one, then co-leads, then leads while the seasoned one is still in the room. Ephesians is explicit about this. The pastors and teachers are given to equip the saints for the work of ministry, which means the leader's job is not to do the ministry but to make the saints able to do it. A church where only the staff are competent has a staff problem disguised as a volunteer problem.

Give people the training, the tools, and the room to grow into the work. A volunteer set up to succeed will serve for a decade. A volunteer thrown into the deep end will serve until they sink, and then they will sit in the back and never raise a hand again, and you will have lost not a slot but a saint.

sections.title: Let People Stop, and Let Them Lead
sections.body:
Two failures bookend the life of a volunteer, and most churches commit both. We never let the gifted ones lead, and we never let the tired ones stop.

The gifted ones we keep as helpers. They could run the whole ministry, but we keep them folding bulletins, because releasing real authority feels like losing control. So they stay small under us and eventually leave for a church that will let them grow. The tired ones we keep forever. There is no honorable way to step down in most churches, no off-ramp, no season of rest, so the only exit is collapse or guilt, and faithful people are forced to choose between burning out and looking like they quit on God.

Build both doors. Build a way up, where proven volunteers are handed real leadership and trusted to carry it. Build a way out, where a person can serve a defined season, finish with honor, and rest without shame. The Levites in Numbers retired from service at fifty and shifted to guarding the work rather than doing it. Even under the old covenant, God built rest into the rhythm of his workers. A church that cannot let its people rest will not have faithful people for long. It will have replacements.

sections.title: You Will Answer for How You Spent Them
sections.body:
There is a sentence in the Gospels that should haunt every leader who recruits. Jesus saw the crowds and had compassion, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. He did not see the crowd as labor for the harvest. He saw them as the harassed. The very next thing he says is pray for workers, but the order matters. Compassion first. Then the work.

We reverse it. We see the work first and the people second, and we spend them accordingly. I have done this. I have asked a tired person to do one more thing because it was easier than recruiting someone new, and I have called my own convenience their joy of service. The volunteers in your church are not a budget line you get for free. They are people the Lord loves, lent to your care for a season, and you will give an account for whether you tended them or used them.

Lead them like you will answer for them. Because you will. The chairs will get set up either way. The question is whether the person who set them up was shepherded or spent. One of those a leader can live with. The other one follows him to the end of his ministry, a long line of faithful people he wore out and never thanked.
